title: Explain the Facade design pattern (a simplified interface to a complex subsystem) with use cases.
shortTitle: Explain the Facade design pattern with use cases
keyPoints: A facade provides one simple, higher-level interface to a complex subsystem of many classes.
The facade coordinates and delegates to subsystem classes; it does not add business logic of its own.
Clients depend on the stable facade interface, not on volatile subsystem internals, reducing coupling.
The facade does not forbid direct access; advanced callers can still use subsystem classes.
An API Gateway in microservices is essentially a facade at the network level.
Keep the facade thin; if it holds real rules it becomes a God object violating single responsibility.
The facade is an excellent place for a single transaction boundary and consistent logging.

s1_definition.oneliner: A facade is one simple front door that coordinates a complicated subsystem behind it, so clients call one easy method instead of wiring together many classes themselves.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Facade** – a structural design pattern that provides a single, simplified, higher-level interface to a complex subsystem of many classes.
- **Delegation** – the facade holds references to subsystem classes and calls them in the correct order; it adds no business logic of its own.
- **Reduced coupling** – clients depend only on the facade's stable interface, not on the volatile internals of the subsystem.
- **Non-intrusive** – the facade offers the easy path for common cases; advanced callers can still use subsystem classes directly.
- **Thin coordinator** – if the facade starts holding real rules, it degrades into a God object.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants a home loan from National Bank of India. Behind the scenes a home loan involves credit-score checks, income verification, property valuation, legal title checks, and disbursement. Rajesh does not want to visit five departments. Instead he goes to one Loan Relationship Manager who coordinates all five departments and comes back with a decision. That relationship manager is the facade: one simple front person hiding a complicated process.

  │  Mobile  │────►│   API     │────► Transfer Service
  │  Client  │     │  Gateway  │────► Account Service

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Facade is a structural pattern that gives clients one simple, higher-level interface to a complex subsystem of many classes. The facade does not add business logic of its own; it coordinates and delegates to the subsystem in the correct order, so clients depend on one easy entry point instead of on many moving parts. That reduces coupling, makes common workflows trivial to call, and lets the subsystem evolve internally as long as the facade's interface stays stable.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj introduced a LoanApprovalFacade with one method that runs five subsystems in the correct order and returns a single decision. When the bank later replaced its in-house credit scorer with an external bureau, they changed only the facade's wiring and not a single caller, because everyone depended on the facade's stable interface.

The key discipline is keeping the facade thin. The moment it starts holding real rules it degrades into a God object. The real logic stays in the subsystem classes; the facade only orchestrates. And the facade is non-intrusive: it offers the easy path for common cases, but advanced callers can still use subsystem classes directly.

Remember one sentence: a facade is one simple front door that orchestrates a complicated subsystem behind it, reducing coupling and making common tasks easy, while the key discipline is keeping it thin so it coordinates without becoming a God object.
